tldr: Kimi k1.5 demonstrates that scaling reinforcement learning with large language models using long context (128k) and improved policy optimization achieves state-of-the-art reasoning performance without complex techniques like MCTS or value functions.
contributions: Long context scaling to 128k with partial rollouts for training efficiency
A simplistic RL framework using a variant of online mirror descent without Monte Carlo tree search, value functions, or process reward models
A length penalty mechanism to address overthinking during RL training
Effective long2short methods using length penalty with long-CoT activations and model merging
Joint multimodal training on text and vision data
methods: The team trained Kimi k1.5 through pretraining, vanilla SFT, long-CoT SFT, and RL stages. They curated an RL prompt set using automatic filters for diverse coverage, balanced difficulty (assessed via model pass rates), and accurate evaluability, while removing easy-to-hack prompts (e.g., multiple-choice, true/false). The RL algorithm uses a variant of online policy mirror descent with off-policy sampling from the reference policy, excluding value networks. They introduced a length reward to penalize excessive response growth, applied curriculum and prioritized sampling strategies, and used automatic test case generation via CYaRon for coding problems.
results: Long-CoT version: 77.5 on AIME, 96.2 on MATH 500, 94th percentile on Codeforces, 74.9 on MathVista—matching OpenAI's o1. Short-CoT version: 60.8 on AIME, 94.6 on MATH 500, 47.3 on LiveCodeBench—outperforming GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet 3.5 by up to +550%. For coding test case generation, approximately 614 out of 1,000 online contest problems did not require a special judge, with 463 producing at least 40 valid test cases.
limitations: Potential reward hacking risk, though mitigated by prompt filtering; the paper notes developing more advanced verification models remains an open direction
Length penalty may slow training during initial phases
The approach relies on verifiable problems with objective evaluation criteria, which excludes certain question types
